questions.text:
The running time of an algorithm is given by:
[latex]T(n)=\left\{\begin{matrix} T(n-1)+T(n-2)-T(n-3), &\text { if } n>3\\ n, &\text{ otherwise}\end{matrix}\right.[/latex]
Then what should be the relation between [latex]T(1),T(2),T(3)[/latex], so that the order of the algorithm is constant?
questions.solution:
If T(1) = T(2) = T(3) = c, then T(4) = c + c [latex]-[/latex] c = c, and by induction every T(n) = c: constant time. Otherwise the differences make T grow.

Answer: T(1) = T(2) = T(3)

questions.text: Given two sorted list of size m and n respectively. The number of comparisons needed the worst case by the merge sort algorithm will be:
questions.solution:
Each comparison outputs one element. In the worst case the lists run out together, so all but the last element need a comparison: m + n [latex]-[/latex] 1.

Answer: m+n-1

questions.text: Which of the following is application of Breath First Search on the graph?
questions.solution:
BFS gives shortest hop distances (used to compute eccentricities and the diameter of an unweighted graph), and 2-colouring by BFS levels tests whether a graph is bipartite.

Answer: Both (A) and (B)

questions.text:
Consider the weights and values of items listed below. Note that there is only one unit of each item.

The task is to pick a subset of these items such that their total weight is no more than 11 Kgs and their total value is maximized. Moreover, no item may be split. The total value of items picked by an optimal algorithm is denoted by [latex]V_{opt}[/latex]. A greedy algorithm sorts the items by their value-to-weight ratios in descending order and packs them greedily, starting from the first item in the ordered list. The total value of items picked by the greedy algorithm is denoted by [latex]V_{greedy}[/latex].
The value of [latex]V_{opt}[/latex]-[latex]V_{greedy}[/latex] is ____________.
questions.solution:
Value/weight: item 4 = 12, item 1 = 6, item 3 = 5, item 2 = 4.
- Greedy: take item 4 (2 kg, 24); item 1 (10 kg) no longer fits; take item 3 (4 kg, 20); item 2 does not fit [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]V_{greedy}=44[/latex].
- Optimal: item 1 alone gives 60 (better than 2 + 4 = 52 or 2 + 3 = 48) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]V_{opt}=60[/latex].

Difference = 60 [latex]-[/latex] 44 = 16

Answer: 16

questions.text:
Consider the following undirected graph G:

Choose a value for x that will maximize the number of minimum weight spanning trees (MWSTs) of G. The number of MWSTs of G for this value of x is ______.
questions.solution:
Edges 1 and 3 (from the top vertex) are always in the MST. The left vertex can be joined by either of its two weight-4 edges: 2 choices. The right vertex is joined by x or 5; with x = 5 both are equally cheap: 2 choices.

Number of MSTs = 2 [latex]\times[/latex] 2 = 4

Answer: 4
